request.query: Nebius raises or cuts GPU prices

results.title: Nebius switches preemptible GPUs to dynamic spot pricing
results.author: Saurabh Khatri
highlights:
Since October 8, 2026, Nebius preemptible GPU prices move with demand, up to every 15 minutes. An H100 starts from $0.79 per GPU-hour, capped one cent below on demand.

By Saurabh Khatri · Published Oct 18, 2026

Nebius stopped charging fixed prices for its preemptible GPU virtual machines on October 8, 2026. Since then, the price of a preemptible B300, B200, H200, H100 or RTX PRO 6000 moves with spare capacity and demand for that GPU type in that region. Nebius announced the change in a blog post on September 22, 2026.

## How the price moves

- The spot price can change as often as every 15 minutes.
- It stays between a floor and a ceiling. The ceiling is one cent below the current on-demand rate for the same GPU.
- The console shows the current price and up to 30 days of price history before you launch.
- The same spot price applies to preemptible capacity in Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

## Old fixed prices and the new range

Per GPU-hour, in US dollars, excluding tax. The spot figures are the minimums that Nebius’s documentation lists; the ceiling follows from the one-cent rule and today’s on-demand prices.

| GPU | Fixed preemptible, before Oct 8 | Spot, from Oct 8 | Spot ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 | $4.30 | from $0.99 | $9.49 |
| B200 | $3.95 | from $0.99 | $8.49 |
| H200 | $2.45 | from $0.79 | $5.39 |
| H100 | $2.15 | from $0.79 | $4.49 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | $0.95 | from $0.79 | $1.79 |

The floor is far below the old fixed prices, but the ceiling is close to the on-demand rate. What you pay depends on demand at the time. The L40S is not part of spot pricing and keeps a flat preemptible rate.

## Two ways to run

- Set a maximum price per GPU-hour for a GPU type and region. Your VM runs while the spot price is at or below it, and you pay the spot price. If the price goes above your maximum, the VM stops and its data is kept. A standalone VM has to be restarted by you or your automation once the price falls; Kubernetes restarts nodes on its own.
- Set no maximum. You pay whatever the spot price is, and you lose the VM only during maintenance or when Nebius reclaims the capacity.

...

Nebius asked customers already using preemptible VMs to choose a price setting before October 8. If you run interruptible training or batch jobs there, set a maximum price. Without one, a busy hour can cost almost as much as an on-demand VM.

results.title: I Keep Buying More Nebius - by James Foord
results.author: James Foord
highlights:
Nebius raised prices again

On October 1, Nebius raised on-demand prices across its main Nvidia GPUs.

Specifically, the B300 went from $7.85 an hour to $9.50, a 21% increase. The older H100, H200, and B200 rose 17% to 20%.

This is actually the second increase this year. Cumulatively, the B300’s on-demand rate is up roughly 56% since May.

This reinforces two key points I highlighted in my last update.

Nebius’s first capacity auction cleared 15% above anything it had charged before for Blackwell chips.

Management also said that it expects short-term deals at $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, and signed the first one in the third quarter.

This pricing power is perhaps the single most bullish thing that could have happened for Nebius, and it reflects what is happening in the market.

GPUs are not losing value as quickly as many analysts expected. Even older models are getting more expensive to rent, and that is Nebius’s bread and butter.

...

Now, it’s important to point out that the October 1 increase applies to on-demand capacity, which is a small share of revenue.

Most of Nebius’s revenue is from long-term contracts that the hike does not reprice.

As such, I am not adding 20% to my revenue forecast, but what the increase does is set the benchmark for capacity Nebius has not sold yet, and for contracts as they renew.

And every pricing data point since my last article is above my base-case assumption, not below it.

results.title: Nebius (NBIS) Has Pricing Power. Its Earnings Don't Show ...
results.author: Maham Fatima
highlights:
Cloud companies don't usually raise prices. Competition in renting out computing power tends to push the other way, with each new chip generation cheapening the last. Yet at the start of this month, Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) reset compute prices on its NVIDIA B300, B200, H200, and H100 virtual machines, the exact hardware AI developers are scrambling to rent.

...

The proof shows up in pricing. In its second-quarter 2026 shareholder letter, the company said pricing for older-generation GPUs rose more than 30% from the first quarter, and deals signed in the quarter averaged above $20 million in revenue per MW. In recent weeks, Nebius also introduced spot pricing for preemptible machines, letting the price of spare capacity float with demand.

...

The company has leaned on shareholders, too, raising roughly $2.8 billion by selling stock through an at-the-market program, even as news that Nebius Group (NBIS) plans to hike prices sent shares rocketing on strong cloud GPU demand. And with Microsoft and Meta anchoring so much of the demand story, a pullback by either would leave a hole that's hard to fill, a concentration risk common among AI infrastructure stocks.

If older GPUs lose economic value faster, Nebius’ liquidity gives it more cushion to absorb faster replacement cycles and to invest in newer hardware without leaning on debt. 

## GPU Rental Prices Are Rising, Even for Older H100s

GPU rental prices are rising across the board, and not just for the newer chips. Nebius is raising its H100 on-demand rental price by 17%, from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour, starting October 1, 2026. 

This marks Nebius’ second price increase this year for the H100s, following an average 29% on-demand increase in May. It is also raising on-demand rentals of the H200, B200 and B300 by 20%, 19% and 21%, respectively. Rental prices for Nvidia’s B300 have seen a larger increase, up around 56% from its pre-May level of roughly $6.10 per hour. 

Nebius increased pricing across Nvidia H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPU instances by 17% to 21% effective Oct. 1. Rising rental rates across multiple GPU generations suggest AI infrastructure demand remains strong and support the thesis that older GPUs may retain economic value longer than many investors expect.

Nebius is not alone in increasing rental pricing for older GPUs. In September, CoreWeave stated that it is contracting new compute capacity at higher prices, while its Q2 earnings call mentioned a six-year old A100 GPU contract running into 2029. As confirmed by CEO Mike Intrator, pricing for prior-generation products is “at or above where it was years ago.” 

This trend is encouraging for neocloud economics. At both companies, GPUs that are four or more years old are commanding higher rentals well beyond the period when they could be considered cutting-edge. 

But it doesn’t settle the depreciation debate. Some of the increase may reflect scarcity rather than durable value: the current HBM and DRAM memory bottlenecks and constrained B300 supply can push up the demand on older chips. Despite the reasons behind the current demand for older GPUs, the real test for neocloud economics lies in their renewal pricing during the final years of this decade.

results.title: Nebius GPU prices rise across the board, up to… · Slicast
highlights:
A notable shift is emerging in the AI computing power market: while cloud providers continue to expand their data centers, rental prices for certain high-end GPUs are not declining with increased supply—they continue to rise.

According to a price adjustment notice sent by Nebius to its customers, effective October 1, 2026, the company plans to increase prices for multiple on-demand GPU instances by approximately 17% to 21%. The proposed hourly rates per GPU are: H100 rising from $3.85 to $4.50 (a 16.9% increase), H200 from $4.50 to $5.40 (20% increase), B200 from $7.15 to $8.50 (18.9% increase), and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50 (21% increase).

This price adjustment sends a significant signal: the pace of growth in AI computing demand may still outstrip the rate at which high-end GPUs, power, and data center capacity are coming online. Unlike traditional cloud computing, the core scarce resources for AI cloud services extend beyond servers to include GPU availability, power access, liquid cooling systems, networking equipment, and data centers capable of supporting high-density racks. If any single component encounters a bottleneck, new computing power cannot be rapidly deployed.

At the Goldman Sachs Technology Conference, Nebius management stated that the company's visibility into customer demand has extended from approximately 18 months to over 24 months, with some customers already reserving compute capacity for the first half of 2028. The company previously conducted price testing for scarce Blackwell capacity, achieving transaction prices approximately 15% higher than previous peak prices and roughly 20% higher than standard sales pipeline quotes.

The significance of Nebius's price increase lies not merely in the ability to charge approximately 20% more per GPU hour, but in confirming that supply and demand in the AI computing market still favor suppliers. A primary past market concern was that simultaneous launches of numerous data centers could eventually lead to GPU leasing market oversupply, potentially resulting in lower utilization rates, extended payback periods, and asset impairment for companies built under assumptions of higher prices. Nebius signals the opposite: the company is raising prices not only for new B200 and B300 models but also for H100 and H200, which have been on the market for years. This indicates that demand extends beyond the latest architecture, with previous-generation GPUs still offering sufficient performance and cost efficiency for model fine-tuning, inference, scientific computing, and certain enterprise workloads.

If implemented successfully without significant declines in GPU utilization, Nebius will achieve two improvements: higher revenue per unit of computing power and potentially higher economic lifespan and residual value for existing GPU assets than previously anticipated.

However, the on-demand price increase will not uniformly raise all of Nebius's revenue by 20%. Large customers typically sign multi-year contracts with fixed prices, minimum purchase volumes, and service terms that cannot be immediately repriced according to new public rates. This adjustment most directly impacts on-demand and short-term compute contracts rather than long-term capacity agreements already signed by clients like Meta.

The price increase may also involve cost pass-through, as NVIDIA systems, networking equipment, power, and data center construction costs may also rise. Therefore, higher capital returns will materialize only if Nebius's unit revenue growth exceeds its unit investment and operating cost growth.

results.title: Nebius Buys a Startup That Kills 'Idle GPU Tax' — Then Raises Its Own GPU Prices the Same Day — machine.net
highlights:
Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) announced October 1 that it acquired Inferize, a 17-person Tel Aviv startup barely ten months old, to fold into Token Factory, its managed inference platform. Nebius did not disclose a price. Israeli outlets CTech and Globes independently pegged the deal at $100 million to $150 million for a company whose public footprint, as of the announcement, was still a waitlist landing page. Inferize's pitch is narrow and technical: a system that snapshots a warmed serving engine's full CPU and GPU state — compiled kernels, CUDA graphs included — and restores it in seconds rather than the roughly 23 minutes a cold GPU normally takes to come back online, a claim based on the company's own single-vendor benchmark against DeepSeek V4 Pro with no independent verification yet published.

...

## The same-day price hike

The complicating fact missing from Nebius's own announcement: its public rate card moved upward the same day. H200 instances went from $4.50 to $5.40 an hour, H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, according to a rate-card comparison published alongside the deal coverage. On an eight-GPU H200 minimum replica, that is roughly $31,500 a month versus about $26,300 before — a $5,200 monthly increase landing on customers' bills the same day Nebius pitched the acquisition as eliminating an 'idle GPU tax.' An efficiency acquisition that reprices the vendor's own costs rather than the customer's rate card is not quite the same thing as the savings story in the press release, and nothing in Nebius's announcement connects the two moves or explains the timing.

...

There's also a gap between what Inferize's technology actually fixes and what customers need fixed. Fast state-restore only solves half of the cold-start problem: Nebius's own billing policy still warns that once GPU capacity is released, 'it may not be immediately available again.' Minimum-replica customers reserve both a warm serving engine and a physical GPU slot; Inferize's snapshot-and-restore addresses the warm-engine half, not the guarantee that a GPU slot is still there to restore onto. Nebius has not published an integration timeline or a shipped feature for Token Factory customers, continuing a pattern from the Eigen AI and Clarifai deals, where neither acquisition changed customer-facing contract terms at the time of announcement.

results.title: Why Hyperscalers Need Nebius (And Not The Other Way Around) (NASDAQ:NBIS) | Seeking Alpha
results.author: Carla Magliocco
highlights:
## Summary

- Nebius rents 12 of its 16 sites, so it avoids the conversion costs and multi-year timelines of competing ex-crypto miners, and monetizes faster.
- GPU rental prices are rising about 20% this month (B300: from $8.10 to $9.70 per hour), and short-term auctions close at $40-50M per MW versus $20-25M for long-term contracts.
- Q2 revenue grew 454% YoY to $582M versus 251% for costs, though losses persist due to depreciation and heavy CAPEX. I believe that at this pace, profitability is a matter of time.
- Hyperscalers building their own capacity (even to rent out the surplus) is the main threat, but as long as compute stays scarce, they depend on Nebius's speed.

results.title: Nebius Stock: 50 Megawatts Secured, GPU Rates Raised, and a $399 Bull Case
results.author: Rafael Müller
highlights:
## Raising Rates While Others Debate Cuts

A day later, Nebius lifted its hourly rates for Nvidia graphics processors. The on-demand price for the widely used H100 rose from $3.85 to $4.50 per hour, while premiums on top-tier models such as the B300 reached as much as 21%.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nebius?

That move carries weight precisely because some market participants have been debating whether GPU rental prices are heading lower. Nebius's decision suggests the opposite: that modern compute remains scarce and that the company holds genuine pricing power.

Software is the second front. Nebius acquired Inferize, a specialist in inference optimization, and will fold both its technology and its development team into the Token Factory platform. The goal is to cut idle GPU capacity and improve the economics of running AI models. No financial terms were disclosed, though industry observers cited by media put the transaction between $100 million and $130 million — with some estimates stretching to $150 million.

results.title: Nebius Stock: Higher GPU Rates, a 12-Year Capacity Deal and the Inference Bet Behind the Headlines
results.author: Rafael Müller
highlights:
## New tariffs, but only for selected instances

As of October 1, published on-demand rates for certain NVIDIA GPU instances moved higher, according to media reports. The price list cites $8.50 per GPU-hour for the B200 and $9.50 for the B300.

The word "selected" carries weight here. This is not a documented price increase across the entire portfolio, and published rates are not the same as realized revenue. The change concerns the terms of the offering, not a reported jump in sales. Investors looking for proof of higher profitability will not find it in a price sheet alone.

On Thursday, Nebius also reached NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud status for training workloads on NVIDIA HGX B300. According to the company, NVIDIA validated the production infrastructure against its reference architecture. That recognition speaks to technical standing, while the tariff update speaks to commercial terms — two distinct signals that happen to arrive in the same week.
